2.text: ance, and says to him, “I have finished!” — “All right!” — “Now I call to

3.text: the great Sea, ‘O Sea, you are great! Turn back the great river that flows

4.text: to the seashore!’ There comes the wind from the sea, great storm, high

5.text: billows. I call to all of you!” He catches the patient by the skin of the

6.text: abdomen. The man who pronounces the incantation keeps his hands on the

7.text: stomach of the patient, pretending that his palms are the billows. With

8.text: these he kneads the abdomen, and massages it. While doing this he says,

9.text: “Here I am cleaning away all rubbish; I make it to be drifted away by the

10.text: water.” Then he falls backward, as if the breath of the great wind from the

11.text: sea had dragged him away. Then the sea begins to ebb; the tide is at the

12.text: lowest. The pebbles, which have been here since very long ago (these are

13.text: in reality his intestines) are bare of water. There is no water near them.

14.text: “I make you into a very dry place; I make you into a dry sandy shore.

15.text: A hairy maggot is rolling on the sand, it rolls into its hair all the rubbish

16.text: from the ground.” Then the man who pronounces the incantation blows

17.text: with all his strength. He smears over with saliva his right palm. He brings

18.text: snow from outside, and makes it melt in his mouth. Then he brings a blade

19.text: of grass, and fastens it to the necklace of the patient. Then he wipes the

20.text: saliva from his palm. Then the people bring the payment. They make a

21.text: diminutive skin bag, and put into it crumbs of sausage, dry leaves instead

22.text: of skins, a little piece of meat, and a tiny strip of thong. The shaman

23.text: takes all these, and carries them home. He carries them to the sacrificing

24.text: place behind his own tent. There he takes out everything. He stabs the

25.text: pieces of sausage with his knife:¹ these are his reindeer for slaughter. He

26.text: scatters the sacrifice to the Being of Incantation (êwg̣aˊnvu-vaˊɪrg̣ɪn), — the
26.note: Compound native term, below the two-page lexicon floor (no handle). Both g's confirmed dotted (g+U+0323) at 4x against a plain contrast; second element matches the ratified corpus form vaˊɪrg̣ɪn (key va'i_rg.i_n, 10 occurrences/9 pages).

27.text: thong, the beads, and the tobacco; then he comes back. The evening

28.text: comes, and they enter the inner room. The next morning they visit the

29.text: patient again. “Halloo! how are you?” — “Indeed, I am a little better!”

30.text: Then the other one fetches a small river,² and puts it into the chamber-vessel

31.text: to be also used afterwards for washing and sweeping the illness. From that

32.text: time on, he begins to improve, and gradually recovers altogether. That is all.

33.text: Told by Keˊᵋulin (man) in the village of Mɪˊs˙qᴀn, 1900.

34.text: (h) For Pain in the Abdomen. When my belly is ailing, I call the

35.text: bear from the Rear Head (the star Vega), and tie him on my belly as a

36.text: belly-protector. Then I say, “O bear! you are strong. Lick my belly; lick

37.text: it and bite it! With your biting allay my pain.” That is all.

38.text: Told by Scratching-Woman (man) at Mariinsky Post, 1900.
